children: Shares of financial advisory firm Lazard
fell 3% in the morning session after the company reported third-quarter financial results that missed analyst expectations on both profit and revenue.

According to a company press release, Lazard reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $0.36 per diluted share alongside GAAP net revenue of $814 million and adjusted net revenue of $805 million. The $0.36 adjusted profit fell $0.08 short of the $0.44 consensus analyst estimate. According to the report, total revenue trailed the projected consensus target of $848.6 million. On a GAAP basis, the firm recorded net income of $29 million, or $0.26 per diluted share. Falling short of Wall Street benchmarks across both top and bottom lines indicated softer advisory and asset management performance, stoking investor concern over near-term fee generation.
The shares were trading at $36.18, down 3.2% from the previous close.
What is the market telling us

Lazard’s shares are somewhat volatile and have had 13 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

The previous big move we wrote about was 8 days ago when the stock dropped 5% on the news that September consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.7% and core inflation topped estimates, reigniting concerns over Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.

The hotter-than-expected data showed headline consumer prices rising 3.7% annually, while core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, reached 2.6%. In the wake of the report, traders raised the implied probability of a central bank rate increase at the next meeting to nearly 44%. The sudden shift in policy expectations pushed Treasury yields higher and triggered volatility across bond markets. Banking leaders pointed out that persistent interest rate uncertainty and Treasury market swings are dampening client trading activity and stalling corporate dealmaking as reported by TheStreet. When borrowing costs remain high and unpredictable, corporations typically hold off on mergers, acquisitions, and debt offerings, creating broad sector-wide pressure on investment banking revenue.

Lazard is down 27.3% since the beginning of the year, and at $36.18 per share, it is trading 36.5% below its 52-week high of $57 from February 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Lazard’s shares 5 years ago would now be looking at only $692.34.
